title: How does Section 174 affect my R&D tax credit claim?
description: Section 174 affects a federal R&D tax credit claim under Section 41 by controlling whether research costs are deducted or capitalized.
summary: Section 174 affects a federal R&D tax credit claim under Section 41 by controlling whether research costs are deducted or capitalized. For U.S. taxpayers, domestic R&E costs are deductible immediately under Section 174A for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, foreign research must be amortized over 15 years, and Section 280C(c) requires reducing the deduction or the credit.

body.text: Section 174 affects a federal R&D tax credit claim under Section 41 by controlling whether research costs are deducted or capitalized. For U.S. taxpayers, domestic R&E costs are deductible immediately under Section 174A for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, foreign research must be amortized over 15 years, and Section 280C(c) requires reducing the deduction or the credit.
Executive Overview: The Statutory Intersection of Deductibility and Credit Claims

The financial outcome of claiming the federal research and development (R&D) tax credit under 26 U.S.C. § 41 is governed directly by how underlying research and experimental (R&E) expenditures are treated under 26 U.S.C. § 174 and the newly enacted Section 174A (Surgent CPE). While Section 41 provides a dollar-for-dollar reduction in tax liability for qualified research activities, Section 174 and Section 174A dictate whether the broader pool of research expenditures must be capitalized and amortized over time or immediately deducted (Parikh Financial).

This statutory interplay determines whether an R&D tax credit claim yields a net immediate cash-flow benefit or whether mandatory capitalization compresses enterprise liquidity by inflating current taxable income. Following the enactment of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), Public Law 119-21, on July 4, 2025, taxpayers operate under a bifurcated regime: domestic R&E expenditures qualify for immediate expensing under Section 174A for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, whereas foreign R&E expenditures remain subject to mandatory 15-year amortization under Section 174 (Surgent CPE; IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28).
1. Statutory Evolution: From Immediate Expensing to TCJA Capitalization and OBBBA Section 174A
Understanding how Section 174 affects an R&D tax credit claim requires distinguishing among three distinct statutory periods:

items: Pre-2022 Immediate Expensing Regime: Prior to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, former Section 174 permitted taxpayers to immediately deduct research and experimental expenditures in the taxable year paid or incurred (IRS Notice 2023-63; IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-8). Specifically, taxpayers could elect under former Section 174(a) to deduct R&E expenditures currently, elect under former Section 174(b) to defer and amortize those expenditures over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month in which benefits were first realized, or elect under Section 59(e) to amortize them ratably over 10 years.

The TCJA Capitalization Mandate (Tax Years Beginning After December 31, 2021, Through 2024): Section 13206(a) of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA), Public Law 115-97 (enacted December 22, 2017), amended Section 174 for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 (IRS Notice 2023-63). Under TCJA Section 174, taxpayers were required to capitalize specified research or experimental (SRE) expenditures and amortize them ratably over 5 years (60 months) for domestic research and 15 years (180 months) for foreign research, beginning at the midpoint of the taxable year in which the expenses were paid or incurred (Surgent CPE; IRS Notice 2023-63).

The OBBBA Bifurcated Regime (Tax Years Beginning After December 31, 2024): Enacted on July 4, 2025, Section 70302 of the OBBBA (Public Law 119-21) added Section 174A to the Internal Revenue Code and narrowed Section 174 to foreign research (Surgent CPE; Madras Accountancy). Under Section 174A(a), taxpayers may currently deduct domestic R&E expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024 (Surgent CPE). Conversely, foreign R&E expenditures receive no relief under the OBBBA and must continue to be capitalized and amortized over 15 years from the midpoint of the taxable year under amended Section 174 (Parikh Financial).

body.text: Strict Disposition Rules for Foreign Research Under Section 174(d)

In addition to retaining the 15-year amortization period for foreign R&E, Public Law 119-21 tightened the rules governing abandoned or retired foreign projects. Under 26 U.S.C. § 174(d), if any property with respect to which foreign research or experimental expenditures are paid or incurred is disposed of, retired, or abandoned during the amortization period, no deduction is allowed with respect to such expenditures on account of such disposition, retirement, or abandonment, and such amortization deduction must continue with respect to such expenditures. Furthermore, for property disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025, Public Law 119-21 clarified that no deduction or reduction to the amount realized is permitted on account of that disposition (Surgent CPE; Adlega). Taxpayers must continue amortizing the capitalized foreign research costs over the remainder of the original 15-year schedule regardless of whether the underlying project fails, is sold, or is permanently abandoned (Surgent CPE).
2. Definitional Asymmetry: How Section 174 and Section 174A Gate and Outscope Section 41 QREs

A central mechanism affecting every R&D tax credit claim is the asymmetric scope between research deductions and capitalization under Sections 174 and 174A and the research credit under 26 U.S.C. § 41.
The Section 174A Gateway Test and Section 41 Qualification Criteria
To claim an R&D tax credit under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), an activity must satisfy four statutory requirements (Parikh Financial):

items: Section 174A Eligibility (The Gateway Test): Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), the expenditures must be eligible to be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under Section 174A (following the OBBBA conforming amendments to Section 41, which replaced the former reference to Section 174 with domestic expenditures under Section 174A).

Technological in Nature: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature—relying on principles of physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science (Parikh Financial).

Business Component: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(2)(B), the application of that information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component (product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention) of the taxpayer (Parikh Financial).

Process of Experimentation: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), substantially all of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation aimed at resolving uncertainty concerning capability, method, or appropriate design (Parikh Financial).

body.text: In practical terms, a company spending $500,000 annually on qualified domestic R&D typically generates $30,000 to $50,000 in federal R&D tax credits (representing an effective 6% to 10% net benefit depending on the calculation method and historical base). Specifically, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4), the statutory Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) rate for a taxpayer with no qualified research expenses in any of the three preceding taxable years is 6% of current-year QREs ($30,000 on $500,000 of QREs), whereas the standard ASC rate is 14% of current-year QREs that exceed 50% of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years, subject to the 21% corporate reduction when electing the reduced credit under Section 280C(c)(2) (Parikh Financial).
Why Section 174 / 174A Captures a Broader Expense Base Than Section 41

While every Section 41 Qualified Research Expense (QRE) must satisfy the Section 174A gateway, Section 174 and Section 174A encompass a far broader pool of expenses than Section 41 allows for the credit (Parikh Financial; Grant Thornton).

Specifically, whereas an erroneous citation to "Treasury Regulation Section 1.172-2(a)(1)" is sometimes misquoted in secondary literature (26 CFR § 1.172-2 governs net operating losses of corporations), the actual regulatory definition of research and experimental expenditures in the experimental or laboratory sense is codified at 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) (eCFR 26 CFR Part 1; IRS Notice 2023-63). Under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), research or experimental expenditures represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense, including all such costs incident to the development or improvement of a product, and expenditures represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense if they are for activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b), credit-eligible QREs are strictly limited to direct in-house research wages, supplies used in the conduct of qualified research, eligible computer rental or cloud computing costs, and 65% of eligible contract research expenses (up to 75% for payments to qualified research consortia under § 41(b)(3)(C) and up to 100% for eligible energy research conducted by eligible small businesses, universities, or federal laboratories under § 41(b)(3)(D)). In contrast, under 26 CFR § 1.174-2 and IRS Notice 2023-63, Section 174 and Section 174A expenditures include indirect and peripheral costs incident to research activities that are entirely excluded from the Section 41 credit base (KBKG; LinkCPA).

body.text: The Software Development Rule: Section 174(c)(3) and Section 174A(d)(3)

This definitional gap is particularly pronounced in software engineering. Under TCJA 26 U.S.C. § 174(c)(3), any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of any software was statutorily treated as a research or experimental expenditure (IRS Notice 2023-63). Under the OBBBA, this rule is carried forward into Section 174A(d)(3) for domestic software development and retained in Section 174(c)(3) for foreign software development (Surgent CPE; Brady Ware). This statutory classification renders Section 5 of Rev. Proc. 2000-50 obsolete for software development expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 (IRS Notice 2023-63; Brady Ware).

Because Section 174(c)(3) and Section 174A(d)(3) sweep in software development costs regardless of whether the work overcomes technological uncertainty under Section 41, software companies must distinguish among three categories (IRS Notice 2023-63; RSM US):

items: Software development meeting the four-part test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d) (and, where applicable, the high threshold of innovation test for internal-use software under § 41(d)(4)(E)), which is eligible for both Section 41 credits and Section 174A domestic deduction;

Software development that does not meet Section 41 technological uncertainty tests—such as planning the development of computer software, designing the computer software or upgrades and enhancements, building a model, writing computer code and converting it to machine-readable code, and testing the software or upgrades and enhancements to the point the software is ready for commercial sale, lease, or license or ready for use in the taxpayer's trade or business under Section 5 of IRS Notice 2023-63—which remains subject to Section 174A (if domestic) or 15-year Section 174 capitalization (if foreign) without generating any Section 41 credit; and

Routine post-release maintenance, customer support, debugging that does not involve upgrades or enhancements, configuring pre-existing software without source code modification, data migration, website content input, and hosting fees, which are excluded from Section 174 and Section 174A and deducted as ordinary business expenses under Section 162 (RSM US; KBKG / Notice 2023-63).

body.text: Section 280C(c) Coordination Between the Credit and the Deduction

Claiming the Section 41 R&D credit directly reduces the allowable Section 174 or Section 174A deduction. Under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(1) as amended by the OBBBA for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, a taxpayer claiming the full Section 41 research credit must reduce its domestic research or experimental expenditures otherwise deductible under Section 174A(a) or chargeable to capital account under Section 174A(c) by the entire amount of the research credit claimed (Madras Accountancy; Surgent CPE). (During the 2022–2024 TCJA window, Section 280C(c)(1) reduced the capitalized Section 174 amount only to the extent the Section 41 credit exceeded the allowable amortization deduction for that year, though OBBBA specifies that its post-2024 amendment creates no inference regarding pre-2025 taxable years.)

Alternatively, under Section 280C(c)(2), a taxpayer may make an irrevocable election on a timely filed original return (including extensions, via Item A on Form 6765) to claim a reduced credit—cut by the maximum corporate tax rate of 21% under Section 11(b), yielding 79% of the gross credit—and retain 100% of the Section 174A deduction without reduction (Parikh Financial; Surgent CPE). Under IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28, small business taxpayers making a retroactive Section 174A election for 2022–2024 were also permitted to make a late Section 280C(c)(2) election or revoke a prior Section 280C(c)(2) election on their amended returns or Administrative Adjustment Requests (AARs) (Falcon Rappaport & Berkman).
3. Cash-Flow Economics of Mandatory Capitalization and Secondary Tax Code Ripple Effects

When R&E expenditures must be capitalized—as was mandatory for all domestic R&E from 2022 through 2024 and remains mandatory for all foreign R&E in 2025 and beyond—the deferral of deductions compresses cash flow and can overwhelm the current-year cash benefit of the Section 41 R&D credit (Parikh Financial).
Hypothetical Worked Example: Capitalization vs. Immediate Expensing on a $1,000,000 R&E Outlay

To illustrate the mathematical mechanics of Section 174 capitalization versus Section 174A expensing, consider a hypothetical C corporation taxed at the statutory 21% federal corporate rate under 26 U.S.C. § 11(b) (Parikh Financial) that incurs $1,000,000 in R&E expenditures during a single 12-month taxable year:

items: Scenario A — Domestic R&E Under Pre-2022 Law or Post-2024 Section 174A Immediate Expensing:
Allowable Year 1 Deduction: $1,000,000 (100% of expenditure) (ECOM CPA).
Unamortized Deferred Balance at Year-End: $0.
Artificial Increase in Year 1 Taxable Income: $0.
Additional Year 1 Federal Cash Tax Liability from Capitalization: $0.
Scenario B — Domestic R&E Under 2022–2024 TCJA 5-Year Capitalization (60 Months with Midpoint Convention):
Annual Full-Year Amortization Rate: $1,000,000 / 5 = $200,000 per year (20%).
Year 1 Midpoint (Half-Year) Convention Deduction: $200,000 × 0.5 = $100,000 (10% of expenditure, or 6 months out of 60 months) (Parikh Financial; IRS Notice 2023-63).
Disallowed / Deferred Year 1 Deduction: $1,000,000 − $100,000 = $900,000.
Resulting Year 1 Taxable Income Increase: +$900,000.
Resulting Year 1 Additional Federal Tax Liability (at 21%): $900,000 × 0.21 = $189,000.
Scenario C — Foreign R&E Under Current Section 174 15-Year Capitalization (180 Months with Midpoint Convention):
Annual Full-Year Amortization Rate: $1,000,000 / 15 = $66,666.67 per year (6.67%).
Year 1 Midpoint (Half-Year) Convention Deduction: $1,000,000 × (6 / 180) = $33,333.33 (3.33% of expenditure, or 6 months out of 180 months) (Adlega).
Disallowed / Deferred Year 1 Deduction: $1,000,000 − $33,333.33 = $966,666.67.
Resulting Year 1 Taxable Income Increase: +$966,666.67.
Resulting Year 1 Additional Federal Tax Liability (at 21%): $966,666.67 × 0.21 = $203,000.00.

body.text: Analysis of Credit Offset: If a taxpayer incurs $1,000,000 in R&E expenses during a period or in a jurisdiction subject to mandatory capitalization, the resulting $189,000 (5-year domestic) or $203,000 (15-year foreign) first-year tax spike can exceed the entire Section 41 R&D credit generated in that year—and for foreign research, Section 41(d)(4)(F) provides zero R&D credit because foreign research is statutorily excluded from Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(F); IRS Notice 2023-63). Furthermore, failure to project and pay quarterly estimated taxes on taxable income inflated by Section 174 capitalization can expose corporations to estimated tax underpayment penalties under IRC Section 6655 (Parikh Financial).
Secondary Ripple Effects Across Domestic, State, and International Tax Provisions
Changes to taxable income caused by Section 174 capitalization or Section 174A acceleration cascade into multiple Internal Revenue Code provisions:

items: IRC Section 163(j) Business Interest Limitation: Section 163(j) limits the deductibility of business interest expense to 30% of Adjusted Taxable Income (ATI) (Joint Committee on Taxation). Capitalizing R&E expenses increases current-year ATI (expanding the Section 163(j) interest deduction ceiling in year one), whereas deducting or accelerating unamortized R&E costs under Section 174A reduces ATI and can tighten the Section 163(j) limitation, although the OBBBA restoration of EBITDA-based ATI (adding back depreciation and amortization) mitigates part of this compression (RSM US; Brady Ware).

State and Local Tax (SALT) Conformity: Because most state corporate income tax regimes use federal taxable income as their starting base, federal capitalization under Section 174 increases state taxable income in rolling-conformity states that conform to the post-TCJA or post-OBBBA Internal Revenue Code, whereas fixed-date conformity states or states that decoupled from TCJA Section 174 require separate state-level Schedule M modifications (RSM US).

Individual Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) Adjustments: Under 26 U.S.C. § 56(b)(2) and Section 59(e), non-corporate taxpayers (such as individuals receiving Schedule K-1s from pass-through partnerships or S corporations in which they do not materially participate) remain subject to 10-year AMT amortization of R&E expenditures unless they elect 10-year regular tax amortization under Section 59(e), creating a critical book-to-tax and regular-to-AMT divergence (Brady Ware).

GILTI and Subpart F Income: For multinational taxpayers with Controlled Foreign Corporations (CFCs), mandatory 15-year capitalization of foreign R&E expenses at the foreign subsidiary level reduces current deductions against tested income and earnings and profits, increasing the U.S. shareholder's Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income (GILTI / Net CFC Tested Income) inclusion under Section 951A and Subpart F income under Section 951, and potentially altering qualification for the GILTI high-tax exception election (RSM US; KPMG).

Foreign Branch Income and Foreign Tax Credits (FTCs): R&E expenses incurred by foreign branches of a U.S. corporation must be amortized over 15 years on the U.S. return, increasing U.S. taxable income in the foreign branch basket under Section 904(d) without a corresponding increase in creditable foreign taxes (RSM US). Conversely, higher U.S. taxable income alters R&D expense allocation and apportionment under 26 CFR § 1.861-17 for FTC limitation purposes and modifies Deduction Eligible Income (DEI) used to compute Foreign-Derived Intangible Income (FDII) deductions under Section 250.

Base Erosion and Anti-Abuse Tax (BEAT): Under Section 59A, because mandatory capitalization reduces current-year non-base-erosion deductions (or defers base-erosion deductions for payments to foreign related parties) and increases regular taxable income, it directly alters whether an applicable taxpayer exceeds the 3% base erosion percentage threshold (2% for certain financial groups) and modifies modified taxable income for BEAT liability calculations (RSM US).

body.text: 4. Navigating the OBBBA Transition: Elections, Unamortized 2022–2024 Balances, and Accounting Method Changes

Under OBBBA Section 70302(f) and IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (released August 28, 2025, modifying Rev. Proc. 2025-23, and subsequently supplemented by IRS Rev. Proc. 2026-32 on September 4, 2026), taxpayers must transition their accounting methods for domestic R&E expenditures beginning after December 31, 2024, and determine how to recover domestic R&E balances capitalized during 2022–2024 (RSM US; KPMG; Cherry Bekaert).
Procedural Rules: Cut-Off Basis vs. Section 481(a) Adjustments and White-Paper Statements

items: Initial TCJA Year (2022) White-Paper Statement and Subsequent TCJA Method Changes: For the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021, IRS Rev. Proc. 2023-11 (modifying Rev. Proc. 2023-8) waived the requirement to file a formal Form 3115 (Application for Change in Accounting Method) and permitted taxpayers to attach a white-paper statement in lieu of Form 3115 implemented on a cut-off basis. For subsequent TCJA years (2023 and 2024), a formal Form 3115 with a modified Section 481(a) adjustment (taking into account only SRE expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021) was required, and IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-8 (effective December 17, 2024) waived the five-year prior-change eligibility rules in Section 5.01(f) of Rev. Proc. 2015-13 to allow automatic Form 3115 method changes to comply with TCJA Section 174 or interim guidance in Notice 2023-63 and Notice 2024-12.

Post-2024 Section 174A Transition and Rev. Proc. 2026-32 Relief: Under OBBBA Section 70302 and IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28, changes to Section 174A methods for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, are treated as initiated by the taxpayer with automatic Commissioner consent and applied on a cut-off basis with no Section 481(a) adjustment (Surgent CPE). However, on September 4, 2026, the IRS issued Rev. Proc. 2026-32, which expanded automatic accounting method change eligibility through tax years beginning before January 1, 2028 (covering 2026 and 2027), removed the prior sunset limitation on automatic accounting method changes for foreign R&E expenditures under Section 174, and clarified how Section 481(a) adjustments interact with the recovery of unamortized domestic R&E expenditures to prevent duplications or omissions for taxpayers that had not properly complied with TCJA Section 174 in prior years (RSM US; Cherry Bekaert).

headers: Strategic & Cash-Flow Implications for R&D Credit Claimants

cells: 1. Immediate 1-Year Acceleration of 2022–2024 Unamortized Domestic Costs
OBBBA § 70302(f)(2); IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28; IRS Rev. Proc. 2026-32
Deduct 100% of remaining unamortized 2022–2024 domestic SRE costs in the first tax year beginning after Dec. 31, 2024 (2025), while expensing new 2025 domestic R&E under § 174A(a).

Maximizes immediate 2025 tax deduction and cash flow relief; may reduce 2025 regular tax liability against which non-refundable Section 41 credits are applied, increasing Section 39 credit carryforwards (Parikh Financial).
2. Ratable 2-Year Acceleration (2025 and 2026)
OBBBA § 70302(f)(2); IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28; IRS Rev. Proc. 2026-32
Deduct remaining unamortized 2022–2024 domestic SRE costs ratably over two taxable years (50% in 2025 and 50% in 2026), while currently deducting new domestic R&E.

Smooths taxable income across 2025 and 2026, helping manage Section 163(j) ATI limits, 80% NOL utilization caps under § 172(a)(2), and current-year Section 41 tax credit absorption (Parikh Financial).
3. Small Business Retroactive Application (2022–2024 Amended Returns / AARs)

Eligible taxpayers (other than tax shelters under § 448(d)(3)) meeting the § 448(c) average annual gross receipts test ($31,000,000 for 2025) could elect to apply § 174A retroactively to tax years beginning after Dec. 31, 2021, via amended returns or AARs.

While Rev. Proc. 2025-28 granted a six-month superseding return extension for 2024 returns, the statutory deadline to file the retroactive small business election closed on July 6, 2026 (or the expiration of the § 6511 refund statute, if earlier); retroactive deduction elections also required coordinating prior-year § 280C(c) credit reductions (Surgent CPE; Brady Ware).
4. Status Quo 5-Year Amortization of 2022–2024 Balances
OBBBA § 70302; Parikh Financial
Make neither the 1-year nor 2-year acceleration election for 2022–2024 balances; continue amortizing those prior costs over their original 5-year schedule while expensing new post-2024 domestic R&E.
Leaves prior capital trapped over the remaining 60-month schedule through 2029, delaying deduction value unless needed to preserve higher current-year taxable income (Parikh Financial).
5. Elective Forward Capitalization of Post-2024 Domestic R&E
Elect under § 174A(c) to capitalize new domestic R&E and amortize over not less than 60 months beginning when benefits are realized, or elect 10-year ratable amortization under § 59(e).

Preserves higher current taxable income to utilize expiring Net Operating Losses (NOLs), absorb non-refundable credits, eliminate individual AMT adjustments, or manage financial metrics (ECOM CPA; Falcon Rappaport & Berkman).

body.text: 5. Technical Mitigation and Optimization Architectures for R&D Credit Claimants
1. Tripartite Cost Segregation and Algorithmic Tracking

Misclassifying routine operational costs as Section 174 expenditures artificially inflates the capitalized base (particularly for foreign operations or 2022–2024 domestic reviews), while under-documenting direct technical activities reduces the Section 41 credit. An effective accounting architecture maps expenditures into three distinct categories:

items: Bucket 1 — Section 41 QREs (and Domestic Section 174A R&E): Direct wages, supplies, eligible cloud computing costs, and 65% of eligible domestic contract research that satisfy all four tests of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d), generating both immediate domestic deductions under Section 174A and the dollar-for-dollar Section 41 tax credit.

Bucket 2 — Non-Credit Section 174 / Section 174A R&E Costs: Indirect costs incident to research under IRS Notice 2023-63 (patent legal fees, allocable lab rent/utilities, research travel, equipment depreciation, non-qualifying software development, the remaining 35% of domestic contract research under order and risk, and 100% of foreign R&E). Segregating domestic from foreign costs by physical location of the research activity is essential so that the 15-year amortization penalty under Section 174 applies strictly to activities conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or U.S. territories and possessions (IRS Notice 2023-63).

Bucket 3 — Routine Section 162 / Section 263A Operational and Production Costs: Quality control testing, efficiency surveys, management studies, consumer surveys, advertising or promotions, acquisition of another's patent or model, literary or historical research (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i)–(vii)), general and administrative department overhead (payroll, HR, accounting, executive management not directly supporting R&E), post-commercial production costs, and routine inventory costs governed by Section 263A (UNICAP), which remain outside Section 174 capitalization (LinkCPA; KBKG / Notice 2023-63).

body.text: 2. Contractual "Order and Risk" and "Substantial Rights" Structuring

In third-party contract research and collaborative arrangements, contractual terms dictate both who must capitalize R&E expenses under Section 174 and who is legally entitled to claim the Section 41 credit:

items: Section 174 Contract Research Rules: Under Section 6 of IRS Notice 2023-63 (as clarified by Notice 2024-12) and 26 CFR §§ 1.174-2(a)(10) and (b)(3), a "research recipient" incurs SRE expenditures only if the research services are performed at the recipient's order and risk. Conversely, a "research provider" incurs SRE expenditures if the provider bears financial risk under the contract (for example, where payment is contingent on successful development) or if the provider retains an independent right to use any resulting SRE product in its trade or business or otherwise exploit it through sale, lease, or license (unless the provider must obtain express permission from the unrelated recipient under Notice 2024-12) (Grant Thornton).

Section 41 Funded Research Exclusion: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d), qualified research excludes any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity. Under established federal jurisprudence (such as Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), and Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000)), a researcher's activities are treated as "unfunded" for Section 41 purposes only if the researcher both retains substantial rights in the research results and bears the financial risk of development failure (meaning payment is contingent on technical success). Reviewing contracts to clearly allocate financial risk of failure and intellectual property rights prevents a company from inadvertently triggering Section 174 capitalization on third-party-funded work while preserving its Section 41 QRE claim on self-funded development (Grant Thornton).

body.text: 3. Liquidity Generation: Federal Payroll Tax Offsets and State Credit Transferability (Kansas Case Study)
When mandatory capitalization or operating losses prevent a company from immediately utilizing non-refundable income tax credits, statutory monetization mechanisms can restore immediate liquidity:

items: Federal Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Offset: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(h) (as expanded by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, Public Law 117-169), a qualified small business (an entity with less than $5,000,000 in gross receipts for the taxable year and no gross receipts for any taxable year preceding the 5-taxable-year period ending with the current year) may elect on Form 6765 and Form 8974 to apply up to $500,000 per year of its Section 41 R&D tax credit against federal employer payroll taxes—specifically up to $250,000 against the 6.2% employer Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI / Social Security) tax under Section 3111(a) and up to an additional $250,000 against the 1.45% employer Hospital Insurance (Medicare) tax under Section 3111(b) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022 (26 U.S.C. § 41(h); Parikh Financial). While certain commercial lenders and specialty finance providers also offer non-statutory working capital advances collateralized by anticipated tax refunds, the Section 41(h) payroll tax election and state-level refundable or transferable R&D credit programs represent the primary statutory liquidity mechanisms codified under U.S. federal and state tax law.

State Credit Transferability — The Kansas K.S.A. § 79-32,182b Framework: At the state level, a prominent statutory monetization model is the Kansas R&D tax credit under K.S.A. § 79-32,182b (amended by 2022 Kansas House Bill 2239, Section 41, effective starting tax year 2023) (Kansas Department of Revenue; Strike Tax Advisory):

Credit Calculation Formula: For tax years 2023 and after, the Kansas credit rate is 10% (increased from 6.5%) of the excess of current-year Kansas QREs (QRE_t) over the average QREs of the current taxable year and the two preceding taxable years (QRE_t-1 and QRE_t-2) (Strike Tax Advisory; Kansas Department of Revenue): Kansas R&D Credit = 0.10 × [ QRE_t − ((QRE_t + QRE_t-1 + QRE_t-2) / 3) ]

Hypothetical Worked Calculation: If a Kansas manufacturer incurs QRE_t = $1,000,000 in the current year, QRE_t-1 = $500,000 in the prior year, and QRE_t-2 = $400,000 two years prior, the three-year average base is ($1,000,000 + $500,000 + $400,000) / 3 = $633,333.33. The excess QRE is $1,000,000 − $633,333.33 = $366,666.67, yielding a 10% Kansas R&D credit of $36,666.67 (Strike Tax Advisory).

25% Annual Utilization Cap and One-Time Transferability: In any single tax year, a taxpayer may utilize at most 25% of the generated credit (plus any applicable carryforward), with unused portions carried forward indefinitely in 25% annual increments (Strike Tax Advisory). Crucially, effective for tax years 2023 and after under K.S.A. § 79-32,182b(d), a taxpayer without a current Kansas income tax liability may execute a one-time transfer of the full credit to any person (applying via Form K-204 and Form K-260 with the Kansas Department of Revenue), enabling immediate cash monetization to offset federal Section 174 liquidity pressures (Kansas Department of Revenue; Strike Tax Advisory).

body.text: 4. Audit Protection Limits and Risk Transfer Ecosystems

Executing Section 174 and Section 174A accounting method changes while claiming Section 41 R&D credits carries substantial IRS audit exposure. Notably, under IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28 and IRS Rev. Proc. 2026-32, taxpayers do not receive standard Rev. Proc. 2015-13 audit protection with respect to expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning before January 1, 2025, when making certain post-2024 method changes (Surgent CPE; Cherry Bekaert). Similarly, IRS Notice 2023-63 and IRS Rev. Proc. 2023-11 denied audit protection for pre-2022 taxable years and for taxpayers that failed to adopt TCJA Section 174 capitalization in their first required taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021.

Combining contemporaneous Section 174A and Section 41 cost-segregation documentation with specialized audit risk management enables taxpayers to capture full federal and state R&D tax incentives while maintaining rigorous compliance with Internal Revenue Service examination standards.
